candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the 'name' of an authorization resource, policy/permission or scope created through the admin REST endpoints (e.g. POST /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{client}/authz/resource-server/resource). A user who is granted delegated/fine-grained authorization management (or any admin able to create such entities) can store a payload such as a element as the entity name. When a higher-privileged admin browses the resource-server pages and clicks Delete, the stored name is interpolated into the dialog HTML and rendered as trusted HTML.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Other legacy dialog paths (kc-modal.html/kc-modal-message.html) use escaped {{message}} interpolation and are not sinks; the same authz file is the only place in themes/ that uses $sce.trustAsHtml together with ng-bind-html. Angular's ng-bind-html does not sanitize when the value is passed through trustAsHtml, so no implicit escaping applies. Entity names are arbitrary strings and I found no server-side sanitization that strips HTML characters. I also considered that this is a legacy console and that the attacker needs an authorization-management permission, which limits the attack surface but does not remove the sink.
candidates.impact: Stored cross-site scripting in the admin console origin. Script can run with the victim administrator's session, enabling privileged admin REST calls, reading tokens/CSRF state, modifying realms/clients/users, and potentially full realm or server compromise. Requires a user with some authorization-management permission as the source of the stored payload.
candidates.prerequisites: Realm/client where the attacker can create or rename authorization resources/policies/scopes (delegated admin or manage-authorization permission), and a victim admin who opens the delete-confirmation dialog for that entity in the legacy admin console. Theme base/admin (old Angular console) must be in use, and the authorization feature must be enabled for the client.
candidates.root_cause: AuthzDialog.confirmDeleteWithMsg/confirmDelete concatenates the caller-supplied entity name directly into an HTML string ('' + name + ' ?') and passes it to openDialog, which calls $sce.trustAsHtml(message) (authz-services.js:84). The dialog template renders that value with ng-bind-html (kc-authz-modal.html:7), so any HTML/script in the name is executed in the admin console origin. The names originate from authorization resource/policy/scope objects fetched from the admin REST API and are never encoded or sanitized in this path.
candidates.title: Stored HTML/script injection (XSS) in legacy admin console authorization delete dialogs
candidates.trace: (1) Entity name is stored via the authorization admin REST API (no HTML encoding server-side). (2) authz-controller.js calls AuthzDialog.confirmDeleteWithMsg($scope.resource.name | $scope.policy.name | $scope.scope.name, ...) at lines 101/131/468. (3) authz-services.js:112-114 (and 129-131) concatenates '' + name + '' into msg. (4) openDialog stores $scope.message = $sce.trustAsHtml(message) at line 84 instead of the normal escaped {{message}} used by kc-modal.html. (5) kc-authz-modal.html:7 renders the value with ng-bind-html, so markup in the entity name executes as script in the admin console origin. (6) Script execution can abuse the logged-in admin's session (admin REST/console actions) and achieve privilege escalation.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution or browser verification was performed; exploitability depends on the exact roles needed to create authorization entities and on the victim opening the delete dialog. I could not verify against upstream history whether this exact code was later changed, and no CVE/CWE ground-truth label was inspected. The snapshot's .ftl templates and js/apps (admin-ui) sources are not present, so template-side and newer-console variants of this issue could not be checked.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 (Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation - stored XSS)

coverage_summary: Scope: 5,889 model-visible files from the assigned snapshot (keycloak-parent 20.0.1, including core, services, server-spi*, model/*, federation, saml-core, adapters, quarkus, themes resources, testsuite providers, examples). The controller's filters skip binary-like files and excluded src/test trees; FreeMarker .ftl templates and the separate js/apps admin-ui project are not present in the snapshot, so those areas could not be reviewed. I inspected Java security-critical paths (TokenVerifier/JWS/HMAC/RSA, RedirectUtils and OIDC endpoints, Broker OIDC/SAML, SAML signature helpers, admin/admin-auth resources, user profile and account REST, recovery codes, WebAuthn, device/CIBA/PAR flows, action tokens, theme resource loaders, gzip cache) and theme/account JS for HTML injection sinks. Only the authz-dialog HTML injection chain met the bar for a single submitted candidate.
limitations: No build, test, scanner, or runtime execution was performed; findings are source-evidence leads only.
No git history, fix commits, patches, or CVE/CWE ground-truth data were inspected per the run rules, so I cannot confirm which upstream issue (if any) this snapshot targets.
The snapshot omits src/test trees, .ftl templates, and the js/apps admin-ui sources, so server-side template XSS and the newer React admin console could not be assessed.

The submitted candidate's exploitability depends on authorization-management permissions and on a victim admin opening the delete dialog; these preconditions were reasoned about statically, not verified.
Broad modules (model/infinispan, model/map, operator, integration, testsuite utilities) were only sampled, not exhaustively reviewed; other vulnerabilities may exist.

rejected_leads.reason: The URL comes from a protocol-mapper configuration that only a client/realm administrator can set, and the HTTPS restriction appears intentionally commented out consistently in PairwiseSubMapperUtils/Validator; the attacker-control story is weaker than the stored XSS and it is admin-only.

rejected_leads.lead: Gzip resource cache path handling uses a canonical-path prefix check without a trailing separator (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/encoding/GzipResourceEncodingProvider.java:39-43), and the cache path is built from the request-controlled theme type/name/path in ThemeResource.java:69
rejected_leads.reason: Prefix-only check is a known weak pattern, but the file is only written when the theme resource producer returns a non-null stream for the same traversal path, and both FolderTheme and ClassLoaderTheme reject traversal, so a practical write outside the cache subtree was not demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Trusted-domain suffix matching (host.endsWith(trustedDomain)) in TrustedHostClientRegistrationPolicy (lines 165-184, 223-245) and ClientUpdaterSourceHostsCondition
rejected_leads.reason: The matching logic is arguably too permissive (evilexample.com matches example.com), but it only applies when an administrator enables the trusted-host client registration policy with '*' entries; evidence of a concrete CVE-level exploit path in this snapshot is insufficient.

rejected_leads.lead: Wildcard redirect-URI matching in RedirectUtils.matchesRedirects (services/.../RedirectUtils.java:178-194) and its pairwise copy; and logout/account-console referrer validation quirks (AccountConsole.java:239-247, AccountFormService.java:1057-1065)
rejected_leads.reason: The wildcard behavior requires an administrator-configured redirect URI ending in '*' (or a historically permissive setting) and the account-console referrer branches fail closed (verification with a null client returns null), so no strong open-redirect/token-theft evidence was established.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML redirect-binding signature verification (SamlProtocolUtils.verifyRedirectSignature) only runs when samlClient.requiresClientSignature() (SamlService.java:299-307)
rejected_leads.reason: This is documented as intentional ('Shibboleth does not sign the document for redirect binding') and no counterexample of an unsigned flow that should have been rejected was proven.

rejected_leads.lead: Recovery authentication codes, WebAuthn, and action-token handlers
rejected_leads.reason: Inspected paths (hashed one-time code consumption, $sce-free token validation, email/old-email checks, required-action handling) matched expected hardening and showed no clear bypass; time-boxed review only.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak source snapshot (keycloak-parent 20.0.1; 5,889 model-visible files after the controller's binary/size/name filters). I traced the highest-value candidate to the legacy Angular admin console: the authorization (Authz) delete dialogs build an HTML string from a resource/policy/scope name and explicitly mark it trusted HTML, which is then rendered with ng-bind-html in the admin console origin. No runnable PoC was executed; this remains a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed exploit. Other leads considered (sector-identifier SSRF, gzip cache path handling, trusted-domain suffix matching, redirect wildcard matching, SAML redirect signature, recovery codes, update-email token) are weaker on attacker control or counterevidence and are listed as rejected.
